A Categorical Approach to DIBI Models
Tao Gu, Jialu Bao, Justin Hsu, Alexandra Silva, Fabio Zanasi

Abstract
The logic of Dependence and Independence Bunched Implications (DIBI) is a logic to reason about conditional independence (CI); for instance, DIBI formulas can characterise CI in probability distributions and relational databases, using the probabilistic and relational DIBI models, respectively. Despite the similarity of the probabilistic and relational models, a uniform, more abstract account remains unsolved. The laborious case-by-case verification of the frame conditions required for constructing new models also calls for such a treatment. In this paper, we develop an abstract framework for systematically constructing DIBI models, using category theory as the unifying mathematical language. In particular, we use string diagrams – a graphical presentation of monoidal categories – to give a uniform definition of the parallel composition and subkernel relation in DIBI models. Our approach not only generalises known models, but also yields new models of interest and reduces properties of DIBI models to structures in the underlying categories. Furthermore, our categorical framework enables a logical notion of CI, in terms of the satisfaction of specific DIBI formulas. We compare it with string diagrammatic approaches to CI and show that it is an extension of string diagrammatic CI under reasonable conditions.



1
Introduction

Conditional independence (CI) is a fundamental concept across various research areas, including programming languages
[
28
,
6
,
21
]
, statistics
[
10
]
, and database theory
[
1
]
, among others. Although specific definitions may vary, the core idea remains straightforward: events
A
and
B
are ‘independent’ when information about one event does not convey information about the other. Furthermore, events
A
and
B
are ‘conditionally independent’ given event
C
if, with knowledge of event
C
, events
A
and
B
become independent. Albeit intuitive, reasoning about conditional independence is an intricate task, leading to extensive research efforts aimed at formalising such reasoning
[
25
,
14
]
.

For probabilistic programs, an extension of standard programs with constructs to sample from distributions, formal methods for (conditional) independence have emerged as powerful tools for program verification.
For instance, Barthe et. al.
[
6
]
introduced Probabilistic Separation Logic (PSL) and applied it to formalise several cryptography protocols, where independence of variables guarantees no leakage of information and thus security of the algorithms.
A follow-up work from Bao et al.
[
5
]

proposed the logic of
Dependence and Independence Bunched Implications
(DIBI),
which enhances PSL with the ability to reason about
conditional
independence. Syntactically, DIBI extends the logic of Bunched Implications (BI)
[
23
,
27
]
, which is the assertion logic underpinning Separation Logic (SL)
[
28
]
and PSL, with a non-commutative conjunction
\mathbin{\fatsemi}
and its adjoints.
Semantically, as in BI, the separating conjunction
*
is interpreted through a partial operation
\oplus
on states, regarded as the parallel composition. In addition, they define a sequential composition
\mathbin{\odot}
to interpret
P\mathbin{\fatsemi}Q
.
Informally,
P*Q
says that
P
and
Q
hold in states that can be separated, and
P\mathbin{\fatsemi}Q
expresses a possible dependency of
Q
on
P
.
Section

3
will review the logic in more details.

Bao et. al
[
5
]
introduced two kinds of semantic models for DIBI logic – probabilistic and relational.
The probabilistic DIBI models
are used to reason about CI of variables in discrete probabilistic computation.
The relational DIBI models
are designed to express join dependency – a notion of conditional independence in database theory and relational algebra – between variables in relational databases.
These two models share many similarities, and the conditions to verify they are models are repetitive. This led Bao et. al.
[
5
]
to conjecture a categorical approach to construct abstract DIBI models that induce these concrete models as instances. This would greatly facilitate the construction of new models.

To solve this conjecture, we start with the observation that, in both the probabilistic and relational DIBI models, the states
resemble
Markov kernels
: they are maps from
input elements to distributions/powersets over output elements. Specifically, the input/output elements are value assignments on a finite set of variables, as an abstraction of program memories or database entries.
Such DIBI states can be identified categorically as morphisms in the Kleisli categories associated to the discrete distribution monad (
definition

15
, for the probabilistic model) or the nonempty powerset monad (
definition

16
, for the relational model).
However, giving a categorical definition for the parallel compositions
\oplus
is difficult.
The previous work
[
5
]
gives
Figure

1(a)
as a pictorial intuition for the parallel composition.
The states are drawn as trapezoids, with the short and long vertical sides representing the input and output domains, respectively.
There, given a blue map
f_{1}
and a red map
f_{2}
, their parallel composition
f_{1}\oplus f_{2}
takes as input the union of their inputs. Then, each
f_{i}
takes its counterpart in the combined input domain and generates an output. Finally these two outputs are combined to be the output of
f_{1}\oplus f_{2}
.
This parallel composition
is partial
because the combination of their outputs is allowed only when the variables overlap in particular ways.
This creates a challenge to capture DIBI models categorically because, in a categorical setting, the domains and codomains of DIBI states are objects, and it is not obvious how to define the overlap of objects used in the parallel composition.

\oplus
\mapsto
f_{1}
f_{2}
f_{1}\oplus f_{2}

(a)

Parallel composition depicted in
[
5
]
.

f_{1}^{\prime}
f_{2}^{\prime}
\mapsto
f_{1}^{\prime}
f_{2}^{\prime}
\oplus
f_{1}
f_{2}
f_{1}\oplus f_{2}

(b)

A diagrammatic representation.

Figure 1
:
Intuition for parallel composition.

Our solution stems from a formalisation of this graphical intuition through
string diagrams
, a pictorial formalism for monoidal categories. String diagrams are widely adopted as intuitive yet mathematically rigorous reasoning tools across different areas of science, see
[
26
]
for an overview.
We formalise the trapezoids intuition in
Figure

1(a)
into string diagrams as in
Figure

1(b)
.
The maps previously embodied as trapezoids now have a fork shape, with some branches being straight lines and some other branches going through boxes.
The boxes represent arbitrary morphisms in the underlying category, and the straight lines represent the identity morphisms. Whereas composition of two DIBI states were hand-waved as two trapezoids tiled together in
Figure

1(a)
, with string diagram we can define it precisely:
the overlap of the two trapezoids is witnessed by the grey wires, and
the composition joins two diagrams side-by-side with the grey wires shared.
We will show in
Section

4
that this string diagram representation yields DIBI models in any category with enough structure to interpret
, namely, Markov categories
[
9
,
13
]
.
Furthermore, in
Section

5
, we will derive several concrete DIBI models as instances.

Additionally, our framework enables a comparison between different characterisations of conditional independence (CI).
The previous work
[
5
]
expresses probabilistic or relational CI in terms of satisfaction of some DIBI formulas.
Since we can construct categorical DIBI models based on any Markov categories, we define a logical notion of CI for morphisms in Markov categories as satisfaction of those DIBI formulas.
In
Section

6
, we investigate the relationship between our ‘logical’ CI and various CI notions based on categorical structures from literature in synthetic statistics
[
9
,
13
]
.

Throughout the paper we fix a countably infinite set of variables
\mathrm{Var}
, use
x,y,z,\dots
for elements of
\mathrm{Var}
, and use
W,X,Y,\dots
for finite subsets of
\mathrm{Var}
.

2
Category Theory Preliminaries

Unless specified, we assume that all monoidal categories we consider are strict and write
\mathit{dom}(f)
and
\mathit{cod}(f)
for the domain and codomain of any morphism
f
.
We write
\langle\mathbb{C},\otimes,\mathsf{I}\rangle
for a (strict) monoidal category, where
\otimes
is the monoidal product and
\mathsf{I}
the unit object of
\mathbb{C}
. If is also symmetric, we write
\sigma_{\mathsf{A},\mathsf{B}}\colon\mathsf{A}\otimes\mathsf{B}\to\mathsf{B}\otimes\mathsf{A}
for the symmetry natural transformation indexed by objects
\mathsf{A}
and
\mathsf{B}
.

As detailed for instance in
[
29
,
26
,
12
]
, morphisms of symmetric monoidal categories have a graphical presentation as string diagrams, where sequential composition and monoidal product are depicted as concatenation and juxtaposition of diagrams, respectively: given morphisms
f\colon\mathsf{X}\to\mathsf{Y}
,
g\colon\mathsf{Y}\to\mathsf{Z}
,
h\colon\mathsf{U}\to\mathsf{V}
,

Our convention is to read string diagrams from left to right, and tensor products from top to bottom. We will sometimes omit object labels in the diagrams when they are evident or irrelevant to the context. Symmetries are indicated with the string diagram
. We call string diagrams consisting solely of combinations of
s
rewirings
: intuitively, they permute the order of the objects.

\mathsf{del}
is natural
if
f

for every morphism
f
. A
Markov category
is a CD category in which
\mathsf{del}
is natural. A CD category
\mathbb{C}

has conditionals
if for each morphism
f\colon\mathsf{A}\to\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{Y}

marginal

f_{|\mathsf{X}}\colon\mathsf{X}\to\mathsf{Y}
(called the
conditional

3
DIBI Logic and its Probabilistic Model

In this section we review the logic of
Dependence and Independence Bunched Implications
(DIBI). For space reasons, we focus on the discrete probabilistic model for DIBI, as introduced in
[
5
]
. The interested reader may refer to
[
5
]
for the relational model, whose construction follows similar steps.

DIBI formulas are defined inductively as follows:

P,Q::=p\in\mathcal{AP}\mid\top\mid I\mid P\land Q\mid P\to Q\mid P*Q\mid P\mathrel{-\mkern-6.0mu*}Q\mid P\mathbin{\fatsemi}Q\mid P\multimap Q\mid P\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\multimap$}}Q

The additive conjunction
\land
is just the standard Boolean conjunction. The multiplicative conjunction
*
states that
P
and
Q
are independent. Both are already present in BI. DIBI extends BI with the non-commutative conjunction
\mathbin{\fatsemi}
1
1

1

Not to be confused with the additive context constructor which is also denoted as
\mathbin{\fatsemi}
in the standard BI literature such as
[
23
,
27
]
.
, where
P\mathbin{\fatsemi}Q
states that
Q
may depend on
P
. The operation
\mathrel{-\mkern-6.0mu*}
is adjoint to
*
, and
\multimap
,
\mathrel{\reflectbox{$\multimap$}}
are adjoints to
\mathbin{\fatsemi}
. DIBI formulas are interpreted on
DIBI
models
, each consisting of a
DIBI frame

on a set of states
A
and a

valuation
function
\mathcal{V}\colon\mathcal{AP}\to\mathcal{P}(A)

that maps an atomic proposition to the set of states on which it is true.
While a BI frame is based on a partial commutative monoid
[
11
]
, a DIBI frame consists of two monoids (one commutative and one not) on the same underlying set, taking care of the two non-additive conjunctions
*
and
\mathbin{\fatsemi}
, respectively.

Definition 1
(
[
5
]
)

A
DIBI frame
is a tuple
\mathcal{A}=\langle A,\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},E\rangle
, where
A
is a set of states,
\sqsubseteq
is a preorder on
A
,
E\subseteq A
are units, and
\oplus,\mathbin{\odot}\colon A\times A\to\mathcal{P}(A)
are partial binary operations
2
2

2

Note that, even though
\mathbin{\odot},\oplus
are also partial in the models considered in
[
5
]
, they have type
A\times A\to\mathcal{P}(A)
in that work. This is because the authors obtain completeness of DIBI logic using a method developed by Docherty
[
11
]
, which only works for the more general type. Because the operations are actually partial rather than non-deterministic, and we are not interested in completeness here, we stick to the more accurate type.
, satisfying the frame conditions in
Figure

2
.

\displaystyle a\oplus b\doteq b\oplus a

(
\oplus
-
Com
)

\displaystyle\exists e\in E\colon a=e\oplus a

(
\oplus
-
UnitExist
)

\displaystyle(a\oplus b)\oplus c\doteq a\oplus(b\oplus c)

(
\oplus
-
Assoc
)

\displaystyle\exists e\in E\colon a=e\mathbin{\odot}a\hskip 8.50012pt

(
\mathbin{\odot}
-
UnitExist
L
)

\displaystyle\exists e\in E\colon a=a\mathbin{\odot}e

(
\mathbin{\odot}
-
UnitExist
R
)

\displaystyle(a\mathbin{\odot}b)\mathbin{\odot}c\doteq a\mathbin{\odot}(b\mathbin{\odot}c)

(
\mathbin{\odot}
-
Assoc
)

\displaystyle e\in E\,\&\,(a\oplus e)\!\Downarrow\!\,\,\Longrightarrow(a\oplus e)\sqsupseteq a

(
\oplus
-
UnitCoh
)

\displaystyle e\in E\,\&\,(a\mathbin{\odot}e)\!\Downarrow\!\,\,\Longrightarrow(a\mathbin{\odot}e)\sqsupseteq a\hskip 8.50012pt

(
\mathbin{\odot}
-
UnitCoh
R
)

\displaystyle e\in E\,\&\,e^{\prime}\sqsupseteq e\Longrightarrow e^{\prime}\in E

(
UnitClosure
)

\displaystyle(a\oplus b)\!\Downarrow\!\,\&~\,a\sqsupseteq a^{\prime}\,\&\,b\sqsupseteq b^{\prime}\Longrightarrow(a^{\prime}\oplus b^{\prime})\!\Downarrow\!\,\&\,(a\oplus b)\sqsupseteq(a^{\prime}\oplus b^{\prime})

(
\oplus
-
DownClosed
)

\displaystyle(a\mathbin{\odot}b)\!\Downarrow\!\,\&\,(a\mathbin{\odot}b)\sqsubseteq c^{\prime}\Longrightarrow\exists a^{\prime},b^{\prime}\colon a^{\prime}\sqsupseteq a\,\&\,b^{\prime}\sqsupseteq b\,\&\,c^{\prime}=(a^{\prime}\mathbin{\odot}b^{\prime})

(
\mathbin{\odot}
-
UpClosed
)

\displaystyle(a_{1}\mathbin{\odot}a_{2})\oplus(b_{1}\mathbin{\odot}b_{2})\doteq(a_{1}\oplus b_{1})\mathbin{\odot}(a_{2}\oplus b_{2})

(
RevExchange
)

Figure 2
:
DIBI frame conditions (with implicit outermost universal quantifiers), where
\!\Downarrow\!
stands for ‘is defined’,
\doteq
means ‘equal when either side is defined’.

The operations
\mathbin{\odot}
and
\oplus
are referred to as the sequential and parallel compositions of states. Intuitively,
a\sqsubseteq b
says that
a
can be extended to
b
, and
E
is the set of states that act as units for these operations.

For capturing conditional independence, atomic propositions
\mathcal{AP}
have the form
{S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}]
, for finite sets of variables
S,T
. Roughly,
{S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}]
means the values of variables in
T
only depend on that of
S
. We now recall the semantics of DIBI formulas, restricting to the fragment that is necessary for the current work.

Definition 2

Given a DIBI model
\langle\mathcal{A},\mathcal{V}\rangle
,
satisfaction
\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}
of
\text{DIBI}_{\{\land,*,\mathbin{\fatsemi}\}}
-formulas at
\mathcal{A}
-states is inductively defined as follows:

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}I
iff
a\in E

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}\top
always

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}({A}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{B}])

iff

a\in\mathcal{V}({A}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{B}])

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}P\land Q

iff

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}P~\text{and}~a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}Q

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}P*Q

iff

\exists b_{1},b_{2}
such that
b_{1}\oplus b_{2}\sqsubseteq a
,
b_{1}\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}P
,
b_{2}\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}Q

a\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}P\mathbin{\fatsemi}Q

iff

\exists b_{1},b_{2}
such that
b_{1}\mathbin{\odot}b_{2}=a
,
b_{1}\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}P
,
b_{2}\vDash_{\mathcal{V}}Q

For a concrete example of DIBI models, we review the probabilistic models.
Let
\mathrm{Val}
be a set of values, to which variables in
\mathrm{Var}
are assigned.
A
memory over
a finite set of variables
X
is a function
\mathbf{m}\colon X\to\mathrm{Val}
, and the
memory space
over
X
is the set of all memories over
X
,
denoted as
\mathbf{M}[X;\mathrm{Val}]
, or
\mathbf{M}[X]
when
\mathrm{Val}
is clear.
Given a memory
\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X]
and a subset
U\subseteq X
, the memory
{\mathbf{m}}^{U}\colon U\to\mathrm{Val}
is the restriction of
\mathbf{m}
to the domain
U
.
Given a set
S
,
\mathcal{D}S
is the set of discrete distributions over
S
; that is, for any
\mu\in\mathcal{D}S
, we have
\mu\colon S\to[0,1]
, the support
\mathrm{supp}(\mu)=\{s\in S\mid\mu(s)>0\}
is finite, and
\sum_{s\in S}\mu(s)=1
.
A dirac distribution
\mu
on an outcome
s
is the distribution
\mu
such that

\mu(s)=1
, and
\mu(s^{\prime})=0
for any
s^{\prime}\neq s
.
Given a distribution
\mu
in
\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[X]
, if
Y\subseteq X
,
we define the marginalisation of
\mu
to
\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
, written as

\pi_{Y}\mu
, by letting
(\pi_{Y}\mu)(\mathbf{m}_{Y})=\sum_{\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X]\mid{\mathbf{m}}^{Y}=\mathbf{m}_{Y}}\mu(\mathbf{m})
.

To capture conditional independence, we now introduce the notion of
probabilistic input-preserving kernels
.

Definition 3
(
[
5
]
)

A
probabilistic input-preserving kernel
(or
probabilistic kernel
for short) is a function
f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]{}\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]{}
satisfying:

(i)

X\subseteq Y
,

(ii)

\pi_{X}\circ f=\eta^{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathbf{M}[X]}
,
where
\eta^{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathbf{M}[X]}(\mathbf{m})
returns the dirac
distribution over
\mathbf{m}
.

The set of all probabilistic kernels is denoted
\mathrm{ProbKer}
.

In words, a probabilistic kernel
f
maps a memory
\mathbf{m}
on
X
to a distribution of memories on
Y\supseteq X
whose support contains only memories
\mathbf{m}^{\prime}
that faithfully extends
\mathbf{m}
(thus the name ‘input-preserving’). Alternatively,
f
can be seen as a conditional distribution
\Pr(Y\!\mid\!X)
where
Y\supseteq X
, such that
\Pr(Y=B\!\mid\!X=A)
is nonzero only if
B
restricted to the domain
X
equals
A
.

Definition 4
(Probabilistic model,
[
5
]
)

The
probabilistic frame
\mathbf{PrFr}[\mathrm{Val}]
based on
\mathrm{Val}{}
is a tuple
\langle\mathrm{ProbKer},\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{ProbKer}\rangle

where
\mathbin{\odot},\oplus,\sqsubseteq
are defined for
arbitrary

f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
and

g\colon\mathbf{M}[Z]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[W]
as:

•

the sequential composition
f\mathbin{\odot}g
is defined iff
Y=Z
. In this case,
f\mathbin{\odot}g
is of the form
\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[W]
, and given
\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X]
,
(f\mathbin{\odot}g)(\mathbf{m})
maps
\mathbf{n}\in\mathbf{M}[W]
to
\sum_{\bm{\ell}\in\mathrm{supp}(f(\mathbf{m}))}g(\bm{\ell})(\mathbf{n})
;

•

the parallel composition
f\oplus g
is defined iff
X\cap Z=Y\cap W
. In this case,
f\oplus g
is of the form
\mathbf{M}[X\cup Z]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y\cup W]
such that given
\bm{\ell}\in\mathbf{M}[X\cup Z]
and
\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[Y\cup W]
,
we have

(f\oplus g)(\bm{\ell})(\mathbf{m})=f({\bm{\ell}}^{X})({\mathbf{m}}^{Y})\cdot g({\bm{\ell}}^{Z})({\mathbf{m}}^{W})
;

•

the subkernel relation
f\sqsubseteq g
holds if there exist a finite set of variables
S
and
h\in\mathrm{ProbKer}
such that
g=\left(f\oplus\eta^{\mathcal{D}}_{\mathbf{M}[S]}\right)\mathbin{\odot}h
.

The
probabilistic model based on
\mathrm{Val}
consists of the probabilistic frame
\mathbf{PrFr}[\mathrm{Val}]
and the following
natural valuation

\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}\colon\mathcal{AP}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathrm{ProbKer})
: given
({S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}])
and
f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
,
f\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}({S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}])
iff there exists a probabilistic kernel
f^{\prime}\colon\mathbf{M}[X^{\prime}]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y^{\prime}]
such that
f^{\prime}\sqsubseteq f
,
X^{\prime}=S
and
T\subseteq Y^{\prime}
.

We may simply write
\mathbf{PrFr}
when the underlying set of values
\mathrm{Val}
is evident.

Next we give examples of probabilistic kernels and how they compose.
We will abbreviate a map from a variable
x
to a value
c
as
c_{x}
and use the ket notation
|\omega\rangle
for each probabilistic outcome
\omega
.

Example 1

Consider variables
x,y,z
that take values in
\mathbf{Val}=\{0,1\}
.
We define a map
f\colon\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[\{x,y,z\}]
by:

\displaystyle f({\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}|0_{x},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{4}|0_{x},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{4}|1_{y},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{4}|1_{y},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle

\displaystyle f({\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{16}|0_{x},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{3}{16}|0_{x},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{3}{16}|1_{y},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{9}{16}|1_{y},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle

The input memory (coloured) is preserved by
f
so it is a probabilistic kernel.
Then define
g_{1}\colon\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[\{x,z\}]
and
g_{2}\colon\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[\{y,z\}]
as:

\displaystyle g_{1}({\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}|0_{x},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}|1_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle

\displaystyle g_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}|0_{x},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{3}{4}|1_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle

\displaystyle g_{2}({\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}|0_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}|1_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle

\displaystyle g_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}})

\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}|0_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{3}{4}|1_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle

Both
g_{1}
and
g_{2}
are probabilistic kernels as well.
The parallel composition
g_{1}\oplus g_{2}
is defined since
\{z\}\cap\{z\}=\{x,z\}\cap\{y,z\}
; in fact, it is easy to verify that
g_{1}\oplus g_{2}=f
.
Moreover,
g_{1}
and
g_{2}
can be obtained by projecting the output of
f
on
\{x,z\}
and
\{y,z\}
, respectively, and we can show
g_{1}\sqsubseteq f
and
g_{2}\sqsubseteq f
.

4
DIBI models in Markov categories

In this section we construct more abstract DIBI models based on categorical structures.
The starting point of our approach is a categorical characterisation of the concrete probabilistic models given above.
In the following, we begin by showing examples of how elements in that model can be reformulated in categorical terms and then formally present our categorical construction of DIBI models.

As we noted in
Section

1
, the probabilistic DIBI kernels can be identified as morphisms in the Kleisli category for the distribution monad
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
(
Definition

15
); however, not all morphisms in
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
are probabilistic DIBI kernels, so we need to define the extra conditions categorically.
Let
\mathbb{MemPr}
be the subcategory of
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
where objects are restricted to memory spaces over
\mathrm{Val}
. That is, the objects are memory spaces
\mathbf{m}\colon X\to\mathrm{Val}
, and the morphisms are maps
f:\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}{\mathbf{M}[Y]}
.
Then, probabilistic kernels are exactly those morphisms in the
\mathbb{MemPr}
that satisfy the input-preserving condition in
Definition

3
.
To visualise the probabilistic kernels, we depict them using string diagrams, which is possible because
\mathbb{MemPr}
is a subcategory of
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
and
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
has the monoidal structure(
Appendix

0.A
).
We also observe that the codomain of an input-preserving kernel
f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[Y]
can be decomposed as
\mathbf{M}[X]\times\mathbf{M}[Y\setminus X]
,
Recall the probabilistic kernel
f
from
Example

1
. Since its codomain
\mathbf{M}[\{x,y,z\}]
can be decomposed as
\mathbf{M}[\{x\}]\times\mathbf{M}[\{y\}]\times\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
, we can draw it as follows:

\scriptstyle{f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{y\}]}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{x\}]}

Intuitively,
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]}
produces two copies of the value of
z
, and the values of
x
and
y
are computed from that of
z
via
\scriptstyle{f^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{y\}]}
\scriptstyle{\mathbf{M}[\{x\}]}
, while the value of
z
gets preserved through a straight wire in the bottom.
As in this example, such copy structure of
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
enables us to capture the ‘input-preserving’ condition of probabilistic kernels generally.

Next we want to express the sequential (
\mathbin{\odot}
) and parallel (
\oplus
) compositions of probabilistic kernels categorically.
The former is exactly the sequential composition of morphisms in
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
.
The parallel composition, however, is
not
the monoidal product
\otimes
in
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
, which is the Cartesian product on objects. By definition, the monoidal product is total, while the parallel composition is partial. Even when the parallel composition is defined, the types of the resulting morphisms do not match. Suppose that the parallel composition of
f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[Y]
and
g\colon\mathbf{M}[U]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[V]
is defined, we have

f\oplus g\colon\mathbf{M}[X\cup U]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[Y\cup V]\quad f\otimes g\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\times\mathbf{M}[U]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[Y]\times\mathbf{M}[V]

The key difference is that parallel composition considers a single memory that can be projected into two pieces, while the monoidal product considers the cartesian product of two pieces of memory, no matter if they agree or not on overlapped variables.
To combine
\mathbf{M}[X]
and
\mathbf{M}[U]
into
\mathbf{M}[X\cup U]
categorically, we note that for disjoint
Z_{1},Z_{2}
,
\mathbf{M}[Z_{1}\cup Z_{2}]\cong\mathbf{M}[Z_{1}]\times\mathbf{M}[Z_{2}]
, therefore

\mathbf{M}[X\cup U]\cong\mathbf{M}[X\setminus U]\times\mathbf{M}[X\cap U]\times\mathbf{M}[U\setminus X]
.
Thus we can illustrate the parallel composition of two probabilistic kernels as in the following example.

Example 2

The probabilistic kernels
g_{1}
and
g_{2}
from
Example

1
– seen as
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
-morphisms – are drawn as the first and second string diagram below respectively.

g_{1}^{\prime}
\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{x\}]

g_{2}^{\prime}
\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{y\}]

g_{1}^{\prime}
g_{2}^{\prime}
\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{x\}]
\mathbf{M}[\{y\}]

where
g_{1}^{\prime}\colon\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[\{x\}]
and
g_{2}^{\prime}\colon\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]\rightarrowtriangle\mathbf{M}[\{y\}]
represent the conditional distributions obtained by suitable projections of
g_{1}
and
g_{2}
, respectively. The parallel composition
g_{1}\oplus g_{2}
is given by the rightmost string diagram above.

We omit the formal string diagrammatic definitions here as they can be easily derived from their counterparts in the generic construction of DIBI models, defined later in
Definition

7
.

Towards that categorical construction of DIBI models,
we also want to generalise the concept of memory spaces

\mathbf{M}[X]
, which were customised for reasoning about probabilistic programs and relational databases.
We observe that the side conditions of the parallel and sequential compositions are all based on comparing the set of variables in the (co)domains, so they only depend on the
X
part in
\mathbf{M}[X]
.
This motivates us to define DIBI states as morphisms in a category whose objects are made of variables in
Definition

5
.

To express finite sets of variables and the union of disjoint such sets in a monoidal category,
in the following we will represent finite sets of variables as lists. We impose a linear order
\preceq
on
\mathrm{Var}
such that indexed variables inherit the order of their indices, e.g.,
x_{1}\preceq x_{2}\preceq x_{3}
.
Let
x\prec y
abbreviate for
x\preceq y
and
x\neq y
.
Then, finite sets of variables can be represented as finite lists of variables ordered by
\prec
, via a translation that we write as
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket
. For instance,
\llbracket\{x_{3},x_{1},x_{3},x_{4}\}\rrbracket=[x_{1},x_{3},x_{4}]
.

Throughout the rest of the section we fix a Markov category
\langle\mathbb{C},\otimes,\mathsf{I}\rangle
, and assignment
\theta\colon\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{C})
of a
\mathbb{C}
-object to each
x\in\mathrm{Var}
.

Definition 5

Let
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
be the symmetric monoidal category whose objects are finite lists of variables, and morphisms
[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]\to[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]
are
\mathbb{C}
-morphisms
\theta(x_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes\theta(x_{m})\to\theta(y_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes\theta(y_{n})
.
Sequential composition is defined as in
\mathbb{C}
. The identity on
[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]
is
\mathit{id}_{\theta x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\theta x_{m}}
.
The monoidal product in
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
– which we also write as
\otimes
with abuse of notation – is list concatenation on objects, and monoidal product in
\mathbb{C}
on morphisms.

Since
\mathbb{C}
is a Markov category, it follows immediately that
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
is also a Markov category.
Sometimes we restrict ourselves to a uniform assignment
\theta
; that is, for some fixed
\mathsf{C}\in\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{C})
,
\theta(x)=\mathsf{C}
for all
x\in\mathrm{Var}
. This is in line with the scenario where a fixed value space
\mathrm{Val}
is used for all variables (see
Definition

3
).
In this case, we write
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
as
\mathbb{C}[\mathsf{C}]
to emphasise the uniform value of the assignment. This category can be seen as the full subcategory of
\mathbb{C}
freely generated by
\mathsf{C}
, but with each occurrence of the generating object named by a variable. The next example shows how the construction in
Definition

5
selects morphisms of
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
that act on memory spaces, among which we have all the probabilistic kernels.

Example 3

Let
\mathbb{C}
be
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
, and
\theta\colon\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D}))
be the constant function
x\mapsto\mathrm{Val}
for all
x\in\mathrm{Var}
. Then there is a full and faithful embedding functor
\iota\colon\mathbb{MemPr}\to\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\theta]
: on objects, given a set
X
,
\iota(\mathbf{M}[X])=\llbracket X\rrbracket
; on morphisms, given
f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
with
X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}
and
Y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\}
, its image
\iota(f)\colon X\to Y
is the composed map
\mathrm{Val}^{m}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbf{M}[X]\xrightarrow{f}\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]\xrightarrow{\mathcal{D}\cong}\mathcal{D}\mathrm{Val}^{n}
, where the isomorphisms are, e.g.,
\mathbf{M}[Y]\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbf{M}[y_{1}]\times\cdots\times\mathbf{M}[y_{n}]\xrightarrow{\cong^{\theta}}\mathrm{Val}^{n}
, using the valuation
\theta(y_{j})=\mathrm{Val}
.

Now that we have abstracted the concept of memory spaces used in concrete DIBI models as objects in Markov categories, the states of DIBI models — the role that in the probabilistic models is filled by probabilistic kernels — takes the form of morphisms in these categories. Next we identify those
\mathbb{C}
-morphisms that constitute the states of DIBI models. We call them the
input-preserving kernels
in
\mathbb{C}
, written
\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta])
.

Definition 6

A
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-morphism
f\colon[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]\to[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]
is a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
input-preserving kernel
(or
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
for short) if
x_{1}\prec\cdots\prec x_{m}
,
y_{1}\prec\cdots\prec y_{n}
, and
f
can be decomposed as follows, where
\sigma
is rewiring:

(1)

In words, a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel is a morphism whose interfaces are essentially finite sets of variables, such that the input is preserved as part of the output (through the upper leg of those
s). The map
f^{\prime}
in (
1
) is referred to as the nontrivial part of the input-preserving kernel.
It follows from
Definition

6
that, for a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel, its codomain
[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]
always subsumes its domain
[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]
; also,
u_{1},\dots,u_{k}
are precisely those
y_{j}
s that are not among these
x_{i}
s. Since the (co)domains of
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel are list presentation of sets, we also write the types of
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels using the corresponding sets, e.g., in (
1
),
f\colon\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}\to\{y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\}
.

Next we define compositions on input-preserving kernels, generalising what we have seen in Example
2
for the probabilistic models.

Definition 7
(Compositions)

Given arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f\colon X\to Y
and
g\colon U\to V
as in
Figure

3(a)
, their
sequential composition

f\mathbin{\odot}g
is defined iff
\mathit{cod}(f)=\mathit{dom}(g)
, in which case
f\mathbin{\odot}g=g\circ f
. Their
parallel composition

f\oplus g
is defined iff
X\cap U=Y\cap V
. Assume
L=\llbracket X\cap U\rrbracket
,
L_{1}=\llbracket X\setminus(X\cap U)\rrbracket
,
L_{2}=\llbracket U\setminus(X\cap U)\rrbracket
,
K_{1}=\llbracket Y\setminus(Y\cap V)\rrbracket
, and
K_{2}=\llbracket V\setminus(Y\cap V)\rrbracket
, then
f\oplus g\colon X\cup U\to Y\cup V
is defined as in
Figure

3(b)
, where all the
\sigma_{i}
s are rewiring morphisms for making the input and output variables
\prec
-ordered.

Note here a benefit of the diagrammatic representation: we can easily identify the memory overlap
\mathbf{M}[X\cap Y]
, as it is depicted a separate wire; with traditional syntax, we would need to apply associativity and commutativity to extract it from
\mathbf{M}[X\cup Y]
.
It is easy to see that kernels are closed under compositions. Also, for curious readers, we note that
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels with their parallel compositions form a
partially monoidal category

[
3
]
. Next we define the subkernel relation.

Definition 8
(Subkernel)

Given two
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f
and
g
, we say
f
is a

subkernel
of
g
– denoted as
f\sqsubseteq g
– if there exist
z_{1},\cdots,z_{n}\in\mathrm{Var}
, a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
h
, and rewiring morphisms
\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}
such that
g
can expressed as on the right-hand side.

The subkernel relation is transitive and reflexive, which can be shown simply by manipulations of the string diagram.
We are finally able to state the main result of this section:
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels and their compositions form a DIBI frame.

Theorem 4.1

\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{C}[\theta])=\langle\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]),\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta])\rangle
is a DIBI frame.

Also, under the natural valuation
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}
, a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
f\colon X\to Y
satisfies
{S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}]
iff there is a subkernel
(f^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\to Y^{\prime})\sqsubseteq f
such that
X^{\prime}=S
and
Y^{\prime}\supseteq T
. Thus:

Corollary 1

(\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]),\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}})
is a DIBI model.

We will see in
Section

5
how to use this categorical construction to derive a wide range of DIBI models. Moreover, it also helps to extract properties of the underlying category that are essential to a specific feature of a DIBI model. Here is an example.

Proposition 1

If
\mathbb{C}
further satisfies that for arbitrary morphisms
f,g
and object
\mathsf{D}
,
f\otimes\mathsf{del}_{\mathsf{D}}=g\otimes\mathsf{del}_{\mathsf{D}}
implies
f=g
, then subkernel is unique given its type in the following sense: if
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f_{1},f_{2}\colon U\to V
are both subkernels of
g
, then
f_{1}=f_{2}
.

Note that the uniqueness of subkernels has been observed already in the context of probabilistic and relational models, see
[
5
, Sect. IV]
.
Proposition

1
reveals the general conditions under which we have this uniqueness for a wider class of DIBI models. In particular, we will see in
Section

5.1
how the probabilistic models meets the conditions of
Proposition

1
.

5
Examples

In this section we provide concrete instances of the categorical construction in
Section

4
. The first example concerns the probabilistic DIBI models.
The remaining examples are new DIBI models. Some of them have been suggested in the DIBI paper
[
5
]
, yet not materialised due to the complexity involved in stating each component and verifying the frame conditions. Within our framework, these steps become much easier to perform.

5.1
Probabilistic (and Relational) DIBI Models

As we sketched in
Example

2
and
Example

3
,
the probabilistic DIBI kernels and

\langle\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})),\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}\rangle
input-preserving kernels
correspond to each other.
We now formally show that the probabilistic DIBI model in
Definition

4
can be recovered from the categorical DIBI model
\langle\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})),\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}\rangle
. Since both models are equipped with the natural valuation
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}
, we focus on the frame part.
To make the correspondence precise, we introduce the category of DIBI frames, as hinted in
[
5
, Sect. III]
.

Definition 9

In
the category of DIBI frames
\mathbb{DibiFr}
, objects are DIBI frames; morphisms
f\colon\langle S,\sqsubseteq_{S},\oplus_{S},\mathbin{\odot}_{S},E_{S}\rangle\to\langle T,\sqsubseteq_{T},\oplus_{T},\mathbin{\odot}_{T},E_{T}\rangle
are functions
f\colon S\to T
that respect all the relations and partial operations: for arbitrary
s,s^{\prime}\in S
,

•

s\sqsubseteq_{S}s^{\prime}
implies
f(s)\sqsubseteq_{T}f(s^{\prime})
;

•

if
s\star_{S}s^{\prime}
is defined, then
f(s)\star_{S}f(s^{\prime})
is defined, and
f(s)\star_{T}f(s^{\prime})=f(s\star_{S}s^{\prime})
, for
\star\in\{\oplus,\mathbin{\odot}\}
;

•

s\in E_{S}
implies
f(s)\in E_{T}
.

It turns out that the function
\iota
introduced in
Example

3
extends to an isomorphism of DIBI frames from
\mathbf{PrFr}[\mathrm{Val}]
to
\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\mathrm{Val}])
.

Proposition 2

\mathbf{PrFr}[\mathrm{Val}]\cong\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\mathrm{Val}])
.

Example 4

The probabilistic kernel
g_{1}\colon\mathbf{M}[\{z\}]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[\{x,z\}]
from
Example

1
corresponds to the following
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\{0,1\}]
-kernel
h_{1}\colon[z]\to[x,z]
– i.e., a
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
-morphism
\{0,1\}\rightarrowtriangle\{0,1\}^{2}
– where:
{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}|0,{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}|1,{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}\rangle
,
{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1}\mapsto\frac{1}{4}|0,{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1}\rangle+\frac{3}{4}|1,{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1}\rangle
.
Diagrammatically,
h_{1}
is of the form
h_{1}^{\prime}
\scriptstyle{z}
\scriptstyle{x}
,
where
h^{\prime}_{1}\colon[z]\to[x]
is the map such that
{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}|0\rangle+\frac{1}{2}|1\rangle
and
{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1}\mapsto\frac{1}{4}|0\rangle+\frac{3}{4}|1\rangle

Similarly, the relational DIBI model from
[
5
]
with the value space
\mathrm{Val}
can be shown to be isomorphic to
\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{P}_{\!i})[\mathrm{Val}])
, where
\mathcal{P}_{\!i}
is the nonempty powerset monad.

5.2
Stochastic DIBI Models

Using our categorical construction, we can derive a notion of DIBI model for continuous probabilistic (stochastic) processes, not previously considered. This is of interest because, as we will later show in
section

6
, it allows to capture conditional independence for continuous probability using DIBI formulas.
We take as underlying category
\mathbb{Stoch}
of stochastic processes, defined as the Kleisli category
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{G})
for the Giry monad on measurable spaces – see
Appendix

0.A
for a full definition. Since
\mathcal{G}
is an affine symmetric monoidal monad,
\mathbb{Stoch}
is a Markov category
[
13
]
.
Applying
Theorem

4.1
to
\mathbb{C}=\mathbb{Stoch}
, we get DIBI frames based on stochastic processes.

Proposition 3

Given an arbitrary map
\theta:\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{Meas})
,

\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{Stoch})[\theta])=\langle\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{Stoch}[\theta]),\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{Stoch}[\theta])\rangle

is a DIBI frame.

We call
\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{Stoch}[\theta])
the
stochastic DIBI frame
based on
\theta
and elements in
\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{Stoch}[\theta])
stochastic kernels.

Example 5

We show a representation of the
Box-Muller transformation
using stochastic kernels.
Consider
\theta
that maps all variable names to the
Borel
\sigma
-algebra over reals
(\real,\mathcal{B}(\real))
.
Define stochastic kernels
g_{1}\colon\varnothing\to\{u\}
and
g_{2}\colon\varnothing\to\{w\}
– both standing for
\mathbb{Stoch}
-morphisms
(\mathbf{1},\{\varnothing,\mathbf{1}\})\to(\real,\mathcal{B}(\real))
, or equivalently, a probabilistic measure on
(\real,\mathcal{B}(\real))
– by
g_{i}(\bullet)=\textsc{Unif}(0,1)
for
i=1,2
, where
\textsc{Unif}(0,1)
is the uniform measure over the interval
(0,1)
. Such a uniform measure over infinite outcomes is
not possible in the discrete probabilistic DIBI model.
Define another stochastic kernel
f:\{u,w\}\to\{u,w,x,y\}
where the value of
x,y

are determined by the value of
u,w
:

f(u\mapsto v_{u},w\mapsto v_{w})=\delta_{v_{u},v_{w},\left(\sqrt{-2\ln u}\cdot\cos(2\pi w)\right)_{x},\left(\sqrt{-2\ln u}\cdot\sin(2\pi w)\right)_{y}}.

Then
h=(g_{1}\oplus g_{2})\mathbin{\odot}f
gives a stochastic kernel
\varnothing\to\{u,w,x,y\}
.
Box-Muller transformation says that
x
and

y
are independent in
h(\langle\rangle)
, despite their seemingly dependence on
u
and
w
. We will explain more on this in
Example

7
.

Comparison with
Lilac

[
21
]
.

Our stochastic DIBI models can be used to reason about independence and conditional probabilities in continuous distributions. A recent work
Lilac
by Li et al.
[
21
]
proposed a BI model for the same goal, yet with some crucial differences in the set-up.

First, the states in Lilac’s BI model are probabilistic space fragments of a fixed sample space, and their variables are mathematical random variables that deterministically map elements in the sample space to values.
In comparison, we treat variables as names that can be associated to values or distributions.
Our stochastic kernels – though not using an ambient sample space – can encode their set-up: we can devise a special variable
\Omega
for ‘the sample space,’ and deterministic kernels from
\Omega
to other variables encode random variables.

Second, to reason about conditional probabilities,
Lilac
want probability spaces to be disintegrable with respect to well-behaved random variables.
To achieve that, they require probability spaces in their model to be extensible to Borel spaces, since disintegration works nicer in Borel spaces.
By working with kernels, which already represents conditional probability spaces, we do not need to impose disintegratability on our DIBI states to reason about conditional probabilities.
For instance, while disintegration is not always possible in the category
\mathbb{Stoch}
, we
can still construct a DIBI model based on
\mathbb{Stoch}
.

Other measure-theoretic probabilistic DIBI models.

The category
\mathbb{Stoch}
is not the only Markov category for
measure-theoretic probability. Another choice is
\mathbb{BorelStoch}
, a subcategory of
\mathbb{Stoch}
obtained by
restricting to standard Borel spaces as objects. It has some nice properties that
\mathbb{Stoch}
does not satisfy, such as having conditionals as mentioned above.

\mathbb{BorelStoch}
is also a Markov category and we can easily instantiate a DIBI model.

Proposition 4

Given any map
\theta\colon\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{BorelStoch})
,

\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{BorelStoch}[\theta])
defined as

\langle\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{BorelStoch}[\theta]),\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{BorelStoch}[\theta])\rangle

is a DIBI frame.

The study of measure theory is also intertwined with topology,
and another category for measure-theoretic probability is
the Kleisli category of the
Radon monad

\mathcal{R}

based on the category of compact Hausdorff spaces
\mathbb{CHaus}
and continuous maps (cf.
Appendix

0.A
), which we will denote as
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R})
.
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R})
is also a Markov category
[
13
]
, so
Theorem

4.1
applies.

Proposition 5

Given any map
\theta:\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R}))
,

\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R})[\theta])
defined as
\langle\mathrm{Ker}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R})[\theta]),\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R})[\theta])\rangle

is a DIBI frame.

A measure-theoretic Markov category not formed as Kleisli categories is the Gaussian probability category

\mathbb{Gauss}

[
13
]
. Its objects are natural numbers, and a morphism
n\to m
is a tuple
(M,\sigma^{2},\mu)
representing the function
f:\real^{n}\to\real^{m}
with
f(v)=M\cdot v+\xi
, where
\xi
is the Gaussian noise with mean
\mu
and covariance matrix
\sigma^{2}
. Its monoidal product is addition
+
on the objects and vector concatenation on morphisms.

\mathbb{Gauss}
differs from
\mathbb{Stoch},\mathbb{BorelStoch}
and
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell_{\mathbb{CHaus}}(\mathcal{R})
in that it does not arise as the Kleisli category associated to some monad. But since it is a Markov category, we can again instantiate DIBI models based on
\mathbb{Gauss}
.

Proposition 6

Given any map
\theta:\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{Gauss})
,

\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{Gauss}[\theta])
defined as
\langle\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{Gauss}[\theta]),\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{Gauss}[\theta])\rangle

is a DIBI frame.

5.3
Syntactic DIBI Models

The DIBI models defined so far all have kernels defined by some processes over memory spaces. It is worth considering a different flavour: purely formal, syntactically generated DIBI models.
We start by defining the underlying category.

Definition 10

\mathbb{SynVar}
is the Markov category freely generated as follows:

•

the generating objects are variables in
\mathrm{Var}
;

•

there is exactly one generating morphism of type
[u_{1},\dots,u_{m}]\to[v_{1},\dots,v_{n}]
for distinct variables
u_{1}\prec\cdots\prec u_{m}
and
v_{1}\prec\cdots\prec v_{n}
, written as string diagrams of the form
\vdots
\vdots
\scriptstyle{u_{1}}
\scriptstyle{u_{m}}
\scriptstyle{v_{1}}
\scriptstyle{v_{n}}
.

In words,
\mathbb{SynVar}
-objects are finite lists of variables (without the requirements of duplicate-free or
\preceq
-ordered); morphisms are diagrams freely concatenated using
,
,
,
, and
\vdots
\vdots
\scriptstyle{u_{1}}
\scriptstyle{u_{m}}
\scriptstyle{v_{1}}
\scriptstyle{v_{n}}
, taken equivalence class modulo the Markov category equations.
The syntactic DIBI frame is based on the category
\mathbb{SynVar}[\mathit{id}]
, where
\mathit{id}\colon\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{SynVar})
is the identity function.

Proposition 7

\mathbf{SynFr}=\langle\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{SynVar}[\mathit{id}]),\sqsubseteq,\oplus,\mathbin{\odot},\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbb{SynVar}[\mathit{id}])\rangle
is a DIBI frame.

Equipped with the natural valuation
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}
, one obtains a DIBI model
\langle\mathbf{SynFr},\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}\rangle
.
We postpone an example of
\mathbb{SynVar}[\mathit{id}]
-kernels till
Section

6
,
Example

9
, in which
\mathbb{SynVar}[\mathit{id}]
-kernels are used to distinguish two notions of conditional independence in Markov categories.

An interesting question for future work is how to extend the syntactic DIBI model to a term model. Typically being initial objects in categories of models, term models play an important role in proving completeness and defining categorical semantics for formal systems, including algebraic theories
[
20
]
, logics
[
30
]

(e.g., Lindenbaum–Tarski algebras)
and type theories
[
18
,
17
]
.
A term model for DIBI could lead to a sound and complete axiomatisation of the specific version of DIBI logic in this paper, whose atomic propositions take the form of
{S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}]
.

6
Conditional independence

DIBI logic is designed for reasoning about CI. The prior work
[
5
]
shows that, conditional independence in the discrete probabilistic models and join dependency in the relational models can be characterised by the same class of DIBI formulas.
Generalising this result, in this section we define a notion of CI on
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels based on formula satisfaction.
Since
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
is a Markov category, we can compare our logical notion of CI with existing categorical definitions of CI in Markov categories
[
9
,
13
]
.

Fix a Markov category
\mathbb{C}
and a map
\theta\colon\mathrm{Var}\to\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{C})
. We define CI in the DIBI model
\langle\mathbf{Fr}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]),\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}\rangle
.

Definition 11
(Conditional Independence)

For any mutually disjoint finite sets of variables
W,X,Y,U
,
X
and
Y
are
DIBI conditionally independent given
W
in a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
3
3

3

Note that
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels with domain
\varnothing
are not to be thought of as maps with empty domains. For instance,
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\theta]
-kernels of the form
\varnothing\to\{x,y\}
corresponds to
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
-morphisms
\mathbf{1}\rightarrowtriangle\theta(x)\times\theta(y)
, which denote distributions over
x,y
.
f\colon\varnothing\to W\cup X\cup Y\cup U
if

f\vDash_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}}({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{W}])\mathbin{\fatsemi}(({W}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{X}])*({W}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{Y}])).

(2)

In this case, we write
X\!\perp\!\!\!\perp_{\!\mathrm{L}}\!Y\!\mid\!W
.

Let us unfold what (
2
) means. Under the natural valuation
\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}
, an atomic proposition of shape
{S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}]
encodes the dependence of
T
on
S
: formally, a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
f\colon X\to Y
satisfies
{S}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{T}]
iff
f
contains some subkernel
f^{\prime}\colon S\to Y^{\prime}
such that
T\subseteq Y^{\prime}
.
So the formula (
2
) requires that
f
is a kernel with empty domain that can be decomposed as
f\sqsupseteq f_{0}\mathbin{\odot}(f_{1}\oplus f_{2})
,
where
f_{0}
determines the value on
W
,

f_{1}
determines the value on
X
given the value on
W
,
f_{2}
determines the value on
Y
given the value on
W
, and
f_{1}
and
f_{2}
do so independently of each other.

We illustrate the formula with examples in the discrete probabilistic DIBI model and the stochastic DIBI model.

Example 6

In the setting of
Example

1
, consider the probabilistic kernel
h\colon\mathbf{M}[\varnothing]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[\{x,y,z\}]
representing the following distribution:

\displaystyle\mu=

\displaystyle\frac{1}{8}|0_{x},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{8}|0_{x},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{8}|1_{y},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle+\frac{1}{8}|1_{y},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}0_{z}}\rangle

\displaystyle+\frac{1}{32}|0_{x},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{3}{32}|0_{x},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{3}{32}|1_{y},0_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle+\frac{9}{32}|1_{y},1_{y},{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}1_{z}}\rangle

Then
h\vDash_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}}({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{z\}}])\mathbin{\fatsemi}(({\{z\}}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{z,x\}}])*({\{z\}}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{z,y\}}]))
, because
h=h_{0}\mathbin{\odot}f=h_{0}\mathbin{\odot}(f_{1}\oplus f_{2})
, where
h_{0}
denotes the uniform distribution
\frac{1}{2}|0_{z}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}|1_{z}\rangle
.

Example 7

Define
g_{1},g_{2},f,h
as in
Example

5
. We want to assert that variables
x
and
y
are independent in the distribution
constructed by Box-Muller Transform.
Independence is a special case of conditional independence in which the set of conditioned variables is empty.
Thus, the goal is to assert
({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\varnothing}])\mathbin{\fatsemi}(({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{x\}}])*({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{y\}}]))
– equivalently,
({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{x\}}])*({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{y\}}])
.

Define
h_{1}:\varnothing\to\{x\}
and
h_{2}:\varnothing\to\{y\}

both as the standard normal distribution
\mathcal{N}(0,1)
.
Clearly
h_{1}\vDash_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}}{\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{x\}}]
and
h_{2}\vDash_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}}{\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{y\}}]
.
Moreover, some non-trivial calculations would show that

(h_{1}\oplus h_{2})\sqsubseteq h
, and consequently we have
h\vDash_{\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{nat}}}({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{x\}}])*({\varnothing}\mathrel{\triangleright}[{\{y\}}])
by definition.

Since the categorical DIBI models are based on Markov categories, we compare our logical notion of CI on kernels with the canonical notion of CI in Markov categories, which defines CI as decomposability of morphisms. In
Definitions

12
,
13
and
14
, a Markov category
\mathbb{X}
is fixed.

Definition 12

An
\mathbb{X}
-morphism
s\colon\mathsf{I}\to\mathsf{W}\otimes\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{Y}

displays the
conditional independence
of
\mathsf{X}
and
\mathsf{Y}
given
\mathsf{W}
if there exist
\mathbb{X}
-morphisms
s_{\mathsf{W}}\colon\mathsf{I}\to\mathsf{W}
,
g_{\mathsf{X}}\colon\mathsf{W}\to\mathsf{X}
,
g_{\mathsf{Y}}\colon\mathsf{W}\to\mathsf{Y}
such that equation on the right holds. We write this as
\mathsf{X}\!\perp\!\mathsf{Y}\!\mid\!\mathsf{W}
.

Example 8

We show an example of this notion of CI in the Markov category
\mathbb{Gauss}
.
Consider morphism
s:\varnothing\to\{w,x,y\}
specified by the tuple

\displaystyle\left(!,\sigma^{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&1\\
1&2&1\\
1&1&2\end{bmatrix},\mu=\begin{bmatrix}0\\
0\\
0\end{bmatrix}\right),\text{where $!$ denotes the trivial map from empty domain. }

That is,
s
takes a length 0 vector and generates a length 3 vector, holding the values of
w,x
and
y
,
with the normal distribution
\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2})
.
This
s
can be decomposed as in
Definition

12

with
s_{w}=(!,0,1)
,
g_{x}=(1,0,1)
, and
g_{y}=(1,0,1)
:
composing
s_{2}
,
g_{x}
and
g_{y}
as in
Definition

12
,
we get
\mathbb{E}(w)=\mathbb{E}(\xi_{w})=0
,

\mathbb{E}(x)=\mathbb{E}(w+\xi_{x})=0+0=0
, and similarly,

\mathbb{E}(y)=\mathbb{E}(w+\xi_{y})=0
, justifying the noise’s mean
\mu
being a zero vector.
For the covariance matrix, let
v=(w,x,y)-(\mathbb{E}(w),\mathbb{E}(x),\mathbb{E}(y))
.
Then

\sigma^{2}=\mathbb{E}(v\cdot v^{T})=\mathbb{E}((w,x,y)\cdot(w,x,y)^{T})
, and one may show that
\sigma^{2}
is equal to the matrix above.

.
One intuitive way to think of the extended superset CI is to view the morphisms as certain computational processes
[
24
]
:
\mathsf{X}
and
\mathsf{Y}
are independent given
\mathsf{W}
in
s
if
s
could be obtained via a computation in which
\mathsf{X}
and
\mathsf{Y}
are computed independently from
\mathsf{W}
(using
g_{1}
and
g_{2}
in (
3
) respectively),
after which some further computation may apply (for which stands the
h
part in (
3
)).

Proposition 9

In Markov categories with conditionals, extended superset CI and Markov CI are equivalent. Therefore, in the context of
Theorem

6.1
, suppose further that
\mathbb{C}
has conditionals, then the three notions of CI – DIBI CI, Markov CI, and extended superset CI – coincide.

7
Conclusion

In this paper we provided a general recipe to construct models for DIBI logic, generalising the previously studied probabilistic and relational models. We adopted string diagrams to best visualise the ‘input-preserving’ property that characterises the states in the models, as well as the compositions and subkernel relations, whose definition would be quite convoluted in non-diagrammatic syntax. Then we derived various new classes DIBI models of interest. Also, we abstractly define a notion of conditional independence in terms of DIBI formulas. As our approach is based on Markov categories, we were then able to compare it with other definitions of CI proposed in the literature.

There are many promising directions for future work. On the logic side, DIBI logic – interpreted in the probabilistic models – was designed to be the assertion logic of Conditional Probabilistic Separation Logic (CPSL). Our categorical construction of a wide class of DIBI models suggests a generalisation of CPSL to obtain program logics in various scenarios beyond probabilistic programs, in the spirit of Moggi
[
22
]
.

The notion of CI we propose can be straightforwardly generalised from Markov categories to copy-delete categories (see
Section

2
). This would allow us to encompass models such as relations with bag semantics in databases
[
8
,
16
]
, sub-probability measures
[
19
]
. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge,
Proposition

8
fails for generic CD categories. Hence, finding appropriate notions of CI in this more general setting remains an open question.

From a categorical perspective, the definition of the category
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
deserves further exploration, from at least two angles.
First, the
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-morphisms may be seen as a “bundle” of the images of some syntactic categories of variables and renaming (similar to
\mathbb{SynVar}
from
Section

5.3
) under suitable functors – usually referred to as ‘models’ in functorial semantics. We would like to make the connection with functorial semantics rigorous in terms of the categorical structures involved.
[
20
,
7
]
.
Second, while the current work represents finite sets of variables using deduplicated finite
\preceq
-ordered lists, towards a more principled treatment, it is worth exploring using nominal string diagrams, a diagrammatic calculus for variables and renaming
[
3
,
4
,
2
]
,
to represent sets of variables.

Appendix 0.A
Background on Monads

We first recall the basic definition of monads. We refer to
[
13
, Sect. 3]
for an overview of the material in this section.
An endofunctor
\mathcal{T}\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
is a

monad
if it has a unit
\eta^{\mathcal{T}}:1_{\mathbb{C}}\to\mathcal{T}
and
a multiplication
\mu^{\mathcal{T}}:\mathcal{T}^{2}\to\mathcal{T}
natural
transformations satisfying certain compatibility conditions.
Every monad
\mathcal{T}\colon\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}
induces a Kleisli category
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{T})
, whose objects are exactly
\mathbb{C}
-objects, and morphisms
\mathsf{X}\to\mathsf{Y}
are
\mathbb{C}
morphisms of type
\mathsf{X}\to\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Y}
, with compositions of
f\colon\mathsf{X}\to\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Y}
and
g\colon\mathsf{Y}\to\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Z}
given by
\mathsf{X}\xrightarrow{f}\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Y}\xrightarrow{\mathcal{T}g}\mathcal{T}\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Z}\xrightarrow{\mu^{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathsf{Z}}}\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Z}
. We will write the morphisms in
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{T})
as
\mathsf{X}\rightarrowtriangle\mathsf{Y}
to distinguish them from their counterpart
\mathsf{X}\to\mathcal{T}\mathsf{Y}
in
\mathbb{C}
. Importantly, if
\mathbb{C}
is a SMC and
\mathcal{T}
is a commutative monad, then
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{T})
is also an SMC
[
18
]
. If
\mathcal{T}
is affine symmetric monoidal, then
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{T})
is a Markov category
[
15
,
9
]
.

In the remainder of this section, we recall the monads used in this paper:
the distribution monad
\mathcal{D}
,
the powerset monad
\mathcal{P}
,
the Giry monad
\mathcal{G}
,
and the Radon monad
\mathcal{R}
.

Definition 15
(Discrete Distribution Monad)

The discrete distribution monad
\mathcal{D}
is an endofunctor on
\mathsf{Set}
.
It maps a countable set
X

to the set of distributions over
X
, i.e., the set containing all functions
\mu

over
X
is satisfying
\sum_{x\in X}\mu(x)=1
,
and maps a function
f:X\to Y
to
\mathcal{D}(f):\mathcal{D}(X)\to\mathcal{D}(Y)
,
given by
\mathcal{D}(f)(\mu)(y)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\sum_{f(x)=y}\mu(x)
.

For the monadic structure, define the unit
\eta
by
\eta_{X}(x)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\delta_{x}
, where
\delta_{x}
denotes the Dirac distribution on

x
: for any
y\in X
, we
have
\delta_{x}(y)=1
if
y=x
, otherwise
\delta_{x}(y)=0
. Further, define
\textsf{bind}\colon\mathcal{D}(X)\rightarrow(X\to\mathcal{D}(Y))\to\mathcal{D}(Y)
by

\textsf{bind}(\mu)(f)(y)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{D}(Y)}\mathcal{D}(f)(\mu)(p)\cdot p(y)
.

Definition 16
(Powerset monad)

The powerset monad
\mathcal{P}
is an endofunctor on
\mathsf{Set}
.
It maps every set to the set of its subsets
\mathcal{P}(X)=\{U\mid U\subseteq X\}
. We
define
\eta_{X}\colon X\rightarrow\mathcal{P}(X)
mapping each
x\in X
to the
singleton
\{x\}
, and
\textsf{bind}\colon\mathcal{P}(X)\to(X\to\mathcal{P}(Y))\to\mathcal{P}(Y)

by
\textsf{bind}(U)(f)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\cup\{y\mid\exists x\in U.f(x)=y\}
.

The next monad is defined on the category
\mathbb{Meas}
of measurable spaces, which consists of measurable spaces
(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})
as objects, and measurable functions as morphisms.

\mathbb{Meas}
is a monoidal category, where the monoidal product on objects and morphisms are given by the product of measurable spaces and measurable functions, respectively. In particular, the monoidal unit consists of the singleton measurable space
(\mathbf{1}=\{\bullet\},\{\varnothing,\mathbf{1}\})
.

Definition 17
(Giry Monad)

The
giry monad

\mathcal{G}
maps
a measurable space
(X,\Sigma_{X})

to another measurable space
(\mathcal{G}(X),\Sigma_{\mathcal{G}(X)})
, where
\mathcal{G}(X)
is the set of probability measures over
X
, and the
\sigma
-algebra
\Sigma_{\mathcal{G}(X)}
is the coarsest
\sigma
-algebra over
\mathcal{G}(X)
making the evaluation function
\text{ev}_{A}:\mathcal{G}(X)\to[0,1]
, defined by
\text{ev}_{A}(\nu)=\nu(A)
, measurable for any
A\in\Sigma_{X}
.
For each measurable function
f:X\mapsto Y
,

\mathcal{G}f:\mathcal{G}X\to\mathcal{G}Y
is defined by
(\mathcal{G}f)(\nu)(B)=\nu(f^{-1}(B))
for
B\in\Sigma_{Y}
.
For the monadic structure,
define the unit
\eta
by
\eta_{X}(x)=\delta_{x}
;
define the bind operator
\textsf{bind}_{X,Y}:\mathcal{G}X\to((X\to\mathcal{G}Y)\to\mathcal{G}Y)
by

\textsf{bind}(\nu)(f)(B)=\int_{X}f(X)(B)d\nu
for
B\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{G}Y}
.

Definition 18
(Radon Monad)

The Radon monad
\mathcal{R}
is a measure monad on the category of compact Hausdorff spaces. If maps a compact Hausdorff space
X
to the set of Radom measures
\mu
on
X
such that
\mu(X)\leq 1
. It maps a continuous map between compact Hausdorff spaces
f:X\to Y
to the push-forward measure
\mathcal{R}(f):\mathcal{R}X\to\mathcal{R}Y
given by
\mathcal{D}(f)(\mu)(y)\mathrel{\mathop{:}}=\mu(f^{-1}(y))
.

For the monadic structure:
we define the unit
\eta
to take a point
x\in X
to the diract distribution
\delta_{x}
solely supported at
x
.
We also define the bind operator
\textsf{bind}_{X,Y}:\mathcal{R}X\to((X\to\mathcal{R}Y)\to\mathcal{R}Y)
by

\textsf{bind}(\nu)(f)(B)=\int_{X}f(X)(B)d\nu
.

The category of stochastic processses
\mathbb{Stoch}
is the Kleisli category of the Giry monad
\mathcal{G}
. It is helpful to explicate its structure.

Definition 19

The symmetric monoidal category of stochastic processses
\mathbb{Stoch}
has the following components:

•

objects are measurable spaces
(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})
;

•

morphisms
(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})\to(B,\Sigma_{\!{B}})
are maps
f\colon\Sigma_{\!{B}}\times A\to[0,1]
satisfying: for arbitrary
T\in\Sigma_{\!{B}}
,
f(T,-)\colon A\to[0,1]
is measurable, and for arbitrary
a\in A
,
f(-,a)\colon\Sigma_{\!{B}}\to[0,1]
is a probability measure;

•

compositions of
f\colon(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})\to(B,\Sigma_{\!{B}})
and
g\colon(B,\Sigma_{\!{B}})\to(C,\Sigma_{\!{C}})
is the map
g\circ f\colon\Sigma_{\!{C}}\times A\to[0,1]
mapping
(U,a)
to
\int_{b\in B}g(U,b)\cdot f(db,a)
;

•

the identity morphism
\mathit{id}
on
(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})
maps
(S,a)\in\Sigma_{\!{A}}\times A
to
1
if
a\in S
, and to
0
if
a\not\in S
;

•

the monoidal product
\otimes
acts on objects as
(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})\otimes(B,\Sigma_{\!{B}})=(A\times B,\Sigma_{\!{A}}\otimes\Sigma_{\!{B}})
, where
\Sigma_{\!{A}}\otimes\Sigma_{\!{B}}
is the smallest sigma-algebra containing
\Sigma_{\!{A}}\times\Sigma_{\!{B}})
;

•

the monoidal product
\otimes
acts on morphisms to obtain product measures. That is,
(U,V)\in\Sigma_{\!{B}}\times\Sigma_{\!{D}}
as follows: given
f\colon(A,\Sigma_{\!{A}})\to(B,\Sigma_{\!{B}})
and
g\colon(C,\Sigma_{\!{C}})\to(D,\Sigma_{\!{D}})
,
f\otimes g\colon\Sigma_{\!{B}}\otimes\Sigma_{\!{D}}\times A\times C\to[0,1]
maps
(U,V,a,c)
to
f(U,a)\cdot g(V,b)
.

Appendix 0.B
Omitted Proofs from
Section

4

This section contains the missing proof of statements in
Section

4
, as well as some useful properties of the
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels and the DIBI model. We stay with the setting in
Section

4
for
\mathbb{C}
,
\mathrm{Var}
, and
\theta
.

Proposition 10

If
\mathbb{C}
is a Markov category, then
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
is also Markovian.
If Markov cateogry
\mathbb{C}
has conditionals, then so does
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
.

Proof

Both follow immediately from the construction of
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
: note that
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-morphisms are
\mathbb{C}
-morphisms.

\square

The following observation says that, in
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels, if one forgets the new variables in the output, then one get exactly identity on the input variables.

Proposition 11

For an arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
f\colon X\to Y
,
(\mathit{id}_{X}\otimes\mathsf{del}_{Y\setminus X})\circ f=\mathit{id}_{X}
.

Proof

where we assume

.

\square

The class of
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels is closed under both parallel and sequential compositions.

Proposition 12

For arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f\colon X\to Y
and
g\colon U\to V
, whenever
f\star g
is defined, the result
f\star g
is also an
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel, for
\star\in\{\oplus,\mathbin{\odot}\}
.

Proof

Suppose
f\mathbin{\odot}g
is defined, then spelling out the definition,
Y=U
,

f\mathbin{\odot}g={\hbox to68.58pt{\vbox to33.66pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 36.06595pt\lower-18.93391pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \hbox to0.0pt{
{

By the assumption on
\mathbb{C}
, this entails
f_{1}=f_{2}

Next, we prove the central result
Theorem

4.1
.
We first present two lemmas that are useful in verifying the DIBI frame conditions.

Lemma 1

For any
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
f\colon X\to Y
, and any
U\subseteq_{\!f}\!\mathrm{Var}
such that
U\cap X=U\cap Y=\varnothing
, by viewing
\mathit{id}_{U}
as a (trivial)
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel,
f\oplus\mathit{id}_{U}
is defined, and
f\oplus\mathit{id}_{U}=\sigma_{2}\circ(f\otimes\mathit{id}_{U})\circ\sigma_{1}
, for some rewiring
\sigma_{1}
and
\sigma_{2}
.

Proof

That
f\oplus\mathit{id}_{U}
is defined follows immediately from the assumption that
X\cap U=Y\cap U(=\varnothing)
.
Then
f\oplus\mathit{id}_{U}=\sigma_{2}\circ(f\otimes\mathit{id}_{U})\circ\sigma_{1}
follows immediately by the definition of parallel composition.

\square

Lemma 2

Two
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f
and
g
satisfy
f\sqsubseteq g
if and only if there exist a set of variables
U
and another
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
h
such that
g=(f\oplus\mathit{id}_{U})\mathbin{\odot}h
.

Proof

This follows immediately from
Lemma

1
, by noticing that taking the parallel composition with
\mathit{id}_{U}
– when viewed as a trivial kernel – is nothing but the monoidal product with
\mathit{id}_{U}
, modulo some rewiring.

\square

Now we are ready to check all the DIBI frame conditions for the syntactic DIBI frame whose states are input-preserving diagrams in the freely generated Markov category of string diagrams. We first restate Theorem
4.1
.
See
4.1

Proof
(Proof of Theorem
4.1
)

We verify all the frame conditions in
Figure

2
for the
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels.
We omit the references to
Lemma

1
and
Lemma

2
when using them.

1.

(

⊕

-Com
). Note that the definition of
\oplus
over
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels does not rely on the specific order of the two kernels, thus commutativity holds; in other words, commutativity of
\oplus
holds by definition.

2.

(

⊕

-UnitExist
).
Given an arbitrary kernel
f
, show there exists a kernel
e
such that
f\oplus e=f
holds. In fact, let
e=\mathit{id}_{[~]}
(where
[~]
is the empty list), which is trivially input-preserving, hence is a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel.
f\oplus e
is defined:
\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(\mathit{id}_{[~]})=\varnothing=\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(\mathit{id}_{[~]})
.
Moreover,
f\oplus\mathit{id}_{[~]}=f
.

3.

(

⊕

-Assoc
).
Given
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f,g,h
, suppose
f\oplus g
and
(f\oplus g)\oplus h
are both defined. We show that
g\oplus h
and
f\oplus(g\oplus h)
are also defined; moreover,
f\oplus(g\oplus h)=(f\oplus g)\oplus h
. The converse holds by a similar argument, hence omitted.

Let’s first show that they are defined. By definition, to verify
g\oplus h
is defined amounts to showing
\mathit{dom}(g)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)=\mathit{cod}(g)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)
. Note that, by
f\oplus g
is defined, we have
\mathit{cod}(g)=\mathit{cod}(f\oplus g)\setminus(\mathit{cod}(f)\setminus(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g)))
. Therefore we can calculate
\mathit{cod}(g)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)
as:

\displaystyle\mathit{cod}(g)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{cod}(f\oplus g)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g)\right)\right)\right)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{cod}(f\oplus g)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)\right)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{dom}(f\oplus g)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)\right)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g)\right)\right)

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{dom}(f\oplus g)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g)\right)\right)\right)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{dom}(f\oplus g)\setminus\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\setminus\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g)\right)\right)\right)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\left(\mathit{dom}(f\oplus g)\setminus\mathit{cod}(f)\right)\cup\left(\mathit{dom}(f\oplus g)\cap(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g))\right)\right)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\left(\mathit{dom}(f\oplus g)\setminus\mathit{dom}(f)\right)\cup\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g)\right)\right)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\left(\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cup\mathit{dom}(g)\right)\setminus\mathit{dom}(f)\right)\cup\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g)\right)\right)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

\displaystyle=\left(\left(\mathit{dom}(g)\setminus\mathit{dom}(f)\right)\cup\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g)\right)\right)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(g)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)

To show that
f\oplus(g\oplus h)
is defined, we first note that a similar argument as that above shows
\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)=\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)
. Then,
\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g\oplus h)=\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g\oplus h)
follows immediately:

\displaystyle\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g\oplus h)

\displaystyle=\mathit{cod}(f)\cap(\mathit{cod}(g)\cup\mathit{cod}(h))

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g)\right)\cup\left(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(h)\right)

\displaystyle=\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g)\right)\cup\left(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(h)\right)

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\left(\mathit{dom}(g)\cup\mathit{dom}(h)\right)

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g\oplus h)

The equivalence of
(f\oplus g)\oplus h
and
f\oplus(g\oplus h)
follows immediately from their diagrammatic presentation.

4.

(

⊙

-UnitExistL
).
We show that for arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
f
, there exists a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel
e_{L}
such that
e_{L}\mathbin{\odot}f=f
.
Suppose
\mathit{dom}(f)=\bar{x}
, then simply define
e_{L}\coloneqq\mathit{id}_{\bar{x}}
, which is also a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel kernel; moreover, it satisfies
e_{L}\mathbin{\odot}f=f\circ\mathit{id}_{\bar{x}}=f
.

5.

(

⊙

-UnitExistR
).
Similar to the (

⊙

-UnitExistL
) case. Suppose
\mathit{cod}(f)=\bar{y}
, then let
e_{R}=\mathit{id}_{\bar{y}}
.
e_{R}
satisfies
f\mathbin{\odot}e_{R}=\mathit{id}_{\bar{y}}\circ f=f
.

6.

(

⊙

-Assoc
).
Note that the sequential operator
\mathbin{\odot}
on
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels is exactly the sequential composition in the category
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
, which is associative by definition.

7.

(

⊕

-UnitCoh
).
For arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f
and
g
such that
f\oplus g
is defined, we show
f\oplus g\sqsupseteq f
.
Following the assumption in
Definition

7
,

is of the following form, where we omit the rewiring for simplicity:

The two parts in dotted boxes are
f
and
\mathit{id}_{\mathit{cod}(f)}\otimes g
(which is also a
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernel), respectively. This witnesses
(f\oplus g)\sqsupseteq f
.

8.

(

⊙

-UnitCohR
). We show that for arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f,g
, if
f\mathbin{\odot}g
is defined, then
f\mathbin{\odot}g\sqsupseteq f
. Given the assumption,
f\mathbin{\odot}g=(f\otimes\mathit{id}_{[~]})\mathbin{\odot}g
, which witnesses that
f\mathbin{\odot}g\sqsupseteq f
.

9.

(
UnitClosure
). Since the set
E
is the set of all syntactic input-preserving kernels in the current DIBI frame, this condition is trivially satisfied.

10.

(

⊕

-DownClosed
). Suppose for two
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels of the form
f\colon X\to Y
and
g\colon U\to V
,
f\oplus g
is defined, and there are two subkernels
f_{1}\sqsubseteq f
,
g_{1}\sqsubseteq g
, where
f_{1}\colon X_{1}\to Y_{1}
and
g_{1}\colon U_{1}\to V_{1}
. The goal is to that
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
is defined, and is a subkernel of
f\oplus g
.
To see
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
is defined, since
\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(f)=\mathit{dom}(f_{1})
and
\mathit{cod}(g_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(g)=\mathit{dom}(g_{1})
, we have:

\displaystyle\mathit{dom}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1})

\displaystyle=(\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(f))\cap(\mathit{cod}(g_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(g))

\displaystyle=(\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1}))\cap(\mathit{dom}(f)\cap\mathit{dom}(g))

\displaystyle=(\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1}))\cap(\mathit{cod}(f)\cap\mathit{cod}(g))

\displaystyle=(\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(f))\cap(\mathit{cod}(g_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g))

\displaystyle=\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1})

Next, we show the subkernel relation
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}\sqsubseteq f\oplus g
. By Lemma
2
, we can assume that
f=(f_{1}\oplus\mathit{id}_{S})\mathbin{\odot}f_{2}
,
g=(g_{1}\oplus\mathit{id}_{T})\mathbin{\odot}g_{2}
, where
f_{2},g_{2}
are also
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels. Then, diagrammatically we have:

Notice that the diagrams in the dotted circle is precisely
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
, therefore
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}\sqsubseteq f\oplus g
.

We can also derive the desired property using some other frame conditions as follows:

\displaystyle f\oplus g

\displaystyle=((f_{1}\oplus\mathit{id}_{S})\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\oplus((g_{1}\oplus\mathit{id}_{T})\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})

\displaystyle=((f_{1}\oplus\mathit{id}_{S})\oplus(g_{1}\oplus\mathit{id}_{T}))\mathbin{\odot}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})

(
RevExchange
)

\displaystyle=(f_{1}\oplus g_{1})\oplus(\mathit{id}_{S}\oplus\mathit{id}_{T}))\mathbin{\odot}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})

\displaystyle\eqref{frameAx:plus-ass},\eqref{frameAx:plus-com}

\displaystyle=((f_{1}\oplus g_{1})\oplus(\mathit{id}_{(S\cup T)})\mathbin{\odot}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})

\displaystyle\sqsupseteq f_{1}\oplus g_{1}

\displaystyle(\text{Def. \ref{def:kernel-leq}})

Crucially, the proof below of (
RevExchange
), (

⊕

-Assoc
), and (

⊕

-Com
) does not rely on (

⊕

-DownClosed
).

f_{1},g_{1},h

f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{1}
is defined and
f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{1}\sqsubseteq h

f_{2}\sqsupseteq f_{1}
,
g_{2}\sqsupseteq g_{1}

f_{2}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2}
is well-defined and is exactly
h
.

It is obvious then that
f_{2}\sqsupseteq f_{1}
and
g_{2}\sqsupseteq g_{1}
; moreover,
f_{2}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2}=h
.

12.

(
RevExchange
).
For arbitrary
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
-kernels
f_{1},f_{2},g_{1},g_{2}
, if
(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\oplus(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})
is defined, then
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
and
f_{2}\oplus g_{2}
are defined as well, and
(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\oplus(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})=(f_{1}\oplus g_{1})\mathbin{\odot}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})
.

We first verify that
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
and
f_{2}\oplus g_{2}
are defined. For
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
, we need to show that
\mathit{dom}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1})=\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1})
. Half of the equation is ‘free’ given the ‘non-decreasing’ nature of the kernels, namely
\mathit{dom}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1})\subseteq\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1})
. So it suffices to prove the other inclusion.
Note that
\mathit{dom}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1})=\mathit{dom}(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})
, so it suffices to show that
\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1})\subseteq\mathit{dom}(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})
, as follows:

\displaystyle\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1})

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(f_{2})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{2})

\displaystyle(\text{Definition of }\mathbin{\odot})

\displaystyle\subseteq\mathit{cod}(f_{2})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{2})

\displaystyle(\text{Definition of kernels})

\displaystyle=\mathit{cod}(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\cap\mathit{cod}(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})

\displaystyle(\text{Definition of }\mathbin{\odot})

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\cap\mathit{dom}(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})

\displaystyle((f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\oplus(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})\text{ is defined})

A similar argument confirms that
f_{2}\oplus g_{2}
is defined.

Next we show that
(f_{1}\oplus g_{1})\mathbin{\odot}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})
is defined, namely
\mathit{cod}(f_{1}\oplus g_{1})=\mathit{dom}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})
, as follows:

\displaystyle\mathit{cod}(f_{1}\oplus g_{1})

\displaystyle=\mathit{cod}(f_{1})\cup\mathit{cod}(g_{1})

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(f_{2})\cup\mathit{dom}(g_{2})

\displaystyle=\mathit{dom}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})

Finally, for the equivalence
(f_{1}\oplus g_{1})\mathbin{\odot}(f_{2}\oplus g_{2})=(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\oplus(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})
we draw their diagrams:

{
