Appendix 0.C
Omitted Proofs from
Section

5

We recall
Proposition

2
, which states the isomorphism between the probabilistic DIBI frames and the categorical DIBI frames based on
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
.
See
2

Proof
(Proof of
Proposition

2
)

Recall the embedding
\colon\mathbb{MemPr}\to\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\theta]
from
Example

3
. We show that the restriction of such
\iota
to probabilistic kernels – a subclass of
\mathbb{MemPr}
-objects – which we also write
\iota
with an abuse of notation witness the desired isomorphism of DIBI frames.
First,
\iota
establish a bijection between probabilistic kernels of the form
\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
and
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\mathrm{Val}]
-kernel of the form
\llbracket X\rrbracket\to\llbracket Y\rrbracket
– recall that
\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket
denotes the list representation of finite sets of variables. For simplicity we assume
X=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}
,
Y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{n}\}
.
Given a probabilistic kernel
f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
, its image
\iota(f)\colon[x_{1},\dots,x_{m}]\to[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]
is a
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
-morphism
\mathrm{Val}^{m}\rightarrowtriangle\mathrm{Val}^{n}
obtained by the composition:

\mathrm{Val}^{m}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbf{M}[X]\xrightarrow{f}\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]\xrightarrow{\mathcal{D}\cong}\mathcal{D}\mathrm{Val}^{n}

where
\cong
is the isomorphism
\mathbf{M}[Y]\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathbf{M}[y_{1}]\times\cdots\times\mathbf{M}[y_{n}]\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{Val}^{n}
. It satisfies
Definition

6
immediately by the input-preserving conditions (see
Definition

3
) of the probabilistic kernel
f
.

Before verifying that
\iota
respects the structure on DIBI frames, for convenience we introduce the notion of
combination
of memories: two memories
\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X]
and
\mathbf{n}\in\mathbf{M}[Y]
are combinable if
X\cap Y=\varnothing
; in this case, their combination
\mathbf{m}\uplus\mathbf{n}
is a memory in
\mathbf{M}[X\cup Y]
, such that

\mathbf{m}\uplus\mathbf{n}\colon(u\in X\cup Y)\mapsto\begin{cases}\mathbf{m}(u)&u\in X\\
\mathbf{n}(u)&v\in Y\end{cases}

Now we show
\iota
respects both compositions. The sequential composition in probabilistic kernels is obviously the Kleisli composition, as already observed in
[
5
]
.
So we focus on the parallel composition. Consider the
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\mathrm{Val}]
-kernels
f,g
from
Definition

7
. Their counterpart probabilistic kernels
\iota^{-1}(f)\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y]
and
\iota^{-1}(g)\colon\mathbf{M}[U]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[V]
does the following:

\displaystyle\iota^{-1}(f)

\displaystyle\colon(\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X])\mapsto\sum_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbf{M}[Y\setminus X]}\iota^{-1}(f^{\prime})(\mathbf{m})(\mathbf{n})|\mathbf{m}\uplus\mathbf{n}\rangle

\displaystyle\iota^{-1}(g)

\displaystyle\colon(\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[U])\mapsto\sum_{\mathbf{n}\in\mathbf{M}[V\setminus U]}\iota^{-1}(g^{\prime})(\mathbf{m})(\mathbf{n})|\mathbf{m}\uplus\mathbf{n}\rangle

where
f^{\prime}\colon X\to(Y\setminus X)
and
g^{\prime}\colon U\to(V\setminus U)
are the nontrivial parts of the kernels
f
and
g
, respectively (see
Definition

6
). The parallel composition of these two probabilistic kernels is as follows, according to
Definition

3
. Given
\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X\cup U]
,
\mathbf{n}\in\mathbf{M}[Y\cup V]
,

\displaystyle\iota^{-1}(f)\oplus\iota^{-1}(g)(\mathbf{m})(\mathbf{n})

\displaystyle=\iota^{-1}(f)(\mathbf{m}^{X})(\mathbf{n}^{Y})\cdot\iota^{-1}(g)(\mathbf{m}^{U})(\mathbf{n}^{V})

\displaystyle=\iota^{-1}(f^{\prime})(\mathbf{m}^{X})(\mathbf{n}^{Y\setminus X})\cdot\iota^{-1}(g^{\prime})(\mathbf{m}^{U})(\mathbf{n}^{V\setminus U})

The probabilistic kernel counterpart of
f\oplus g
is:

\displaystyle\iota^{-1}(f\oplus g)\colon

\displaystyle(\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X\cup U])

\displaystyle\mapsto\sum_{\bm{\ell}_{1}\in\mathbf{M}[Y\setminus X],\bm{\ell}_{2}\in\mathbf{M}[V\setminus U]}\iota^{-1}(f^{\prime})(\mathbf{m}^{X})(\bm{\ell}_{1})\cdot\iota^{-1}(g^{\prime})(\mathbf{m}^{U})(\bm{\ell}_{2})|\mathbf{m}\uplus\bm{\ell}_{1}\uplus\bm{\ell}_{2}\rangle

That is, for arbitrary
\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{M}[X\cup U]
and
\mathbf{n}\in\mathbf{M}[Y\cup V]
,

\iota^{-1}(f\oplus g)(\mathbf{m})(\mathbf{n})=\iota^{-1}(f^{\prime})(\mathbf{m}^{X})(\mathbf{n}^{Y\setminus X})\cdot\iota^{-1}(g^{\prime})(\mathbf{m}^{U})(\mathbf{n}^{V\setminus U})

Therefore
\iota^{-1}(f)\oplus\iota^{-1}(g)=\iota^{-1}(f\oplus g)
.

Finally, as the subkernel relation is defined in terms of the sequential and parallel compositions in the same way for both the probabilistic kernels and
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\mathrm{Val}]
kernels,
\iota
also respects the subkernel relation. Therefore we can conclude that
\mathbf{PrFr}[\mathrm{Val}]
and
\mathbf{Fr}(\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})[\mathrm{Val}])
are isomorphic as DIBI frames.

\square

Appendix 0.D
Partially Monoidal Categories

In this section we prove that in the DIBI frames constructed via our recipe, the parallel composition forms a partially monoidal structure. We formalise the result using the notion of partially monoidal categories
[
3
]
.

A
partial monoid

\langle A,e,\diamond,D\rangle
consists of a domain
D\subseteq A\times A
, a binary operation
\diamond\colon D\to A
whose (partial) unit is
e\in D
, such that the monoidal equations hold whenever defined:
(a\diamond b)\diamond c\doteq a\diamond(b\diamond c)
and
e\diamond a=a=a\diamond e
, where
\doteq
stands for ‘equal when either side is defined’.

Definition 20
(
[
3
]
)

A
(strict) partially monoidal category (PMC)
consists of:

•

a small category
\mathbb{C}
with sets of objects
\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{C})
and sets of morphisms
\mathbf{mor}(\mathbb{C})
;

•

partial monoids
\langle\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{C}),\mathsf{E}_{0},\otimes_{0},D_{0}\rangle
and
\langle\mathbf{mor}(\mathbb{C}),\mathsf{E}_{1},\otimes_{1},D_{1}\rangle
, such that
\mathbb{D}
with objects from
D_{0}
and morphisms from
D_{1}
is a subcategory of
\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}
;

•

the operator
\otimes
defined as
\otimes_{0}
on objects and
\otimes_{1}
on morphisms forms a functor
\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}
.

Intuitively, a PMC is a category with compatible partial monoid structures on both the sets of objects and morphisms.

We familiarise the notion of PMC with the probabilistic DIBI models.

Proposition 14

\langle\mathbb{PrKern},\oplus,\mathit{id}_{\mathbf{M}[\varnothing]}\rangle
is a partially monoidal category, where
\mathbb{PrKern}
is the category of probabilistic kernels viewed as a subcategory of
\mathcal{K}\mkern-2.0mu\ell(\mathcal{D})
.

Proof

Let us define the partial monoids on the set of objects and morphisms, respectively.

On objects, the partial monoid
\langle\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{PrKern}),\mathsf{E}_{0},\otimes_{0},D_{0}\rangle
is indeed total:
D_{0}=\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{PrKern})\times\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{PrKern})
; given
\mathbf{M}[X]
and
\mathbf{M}[Y]
,
\mathbf{M}[X]\otimes_{0}\mathbf{M}[Y]=\mathbf{M}[X\cup Y]
;
\mathsf{E}_{0}=\mathbf{M}[\varnothing]
.

On morphisms, define
D_{1}\subseteq\mathbf{mor}(\mathbb{PrKern})\times\mathbf{mor}(\mathbb{PrKern})
to consist of precisely those probabilistic kernels that are parallelly composable; that is, a pair of morphisms
(f\colon\mathbf{M}[X]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[Y],g\colon\mathbf{M}[U]\to\mathcal{D}\mathbf{M}[V])\in D_{1}
iff
X\cap U=Y\cap V
. In this case,
f\otimes_{1}g
is
f\oplus g
. The unit
\mathsf{E}_{1}
is
\mathit{id}_{\varnothing}
.

It remains to verify that
\langle D_{0},D_{1}\rangle
forms a subcategory of
\mathbb{PrKern}\times\mathbb{PrKern}
– denoted
\mathbb{D}
, and
\oplus
is a functor
\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{PrKern}
.

For the former, note that if
f_{1}\oplus g_{1}
and
f_{2}\oplus g_{2}
are both defined,
f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2}
and
g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2}
are both defined, then
(f_{1}\mathbin{\odot}f_{2})\oplus(g_{1}\mathbin{\odot}g_{2})
is also defined by (
RevExchange
).
Also, the identity morphisms are present in
D_{1}
. Therefore
\langle D_{0},D_{1}\rangle
forms a subcategory
\mathbb{D}
of
\mathbb{PrKern}
.

For the latter, the functoriality spells out as: given arbitrary
(f_{1},g_{1}),(f_{2},g_{2})\in\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{D})=D_{1}\times D_{1}
that are sequentially composable,
(g_{1}\circ f_{1})\oplus(g_{2}\circ f_{2})=(g_{1}\oplus g_{2})\circ(f_{1}\oplus f_{2})
. This is guaranteed by (
RevExchange
).

Therefore
\langle\mathbb{PrKern},\oplus,\mathit{id}_{\mathbf{M}[\varnothing]}\rangle
is a PMC.

\square

Proposition 15

\langle\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]),\oplus,\mathit{id}_{[~]}\rangle
is a partially monoidal category.

Proof

The proof is similar to that of
Proposition

14
, which is a concrete case of the current proposition.

We define the partial monoids on the set of objects and morphisms as follows.

For objects, its partial monoid structure
\langle D_{0},\otimes_{0},\mathsf{E}_{0}\rangle
is total:
D_{0}
is simply
\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]))\times\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]))
, namely pairs of list representation of finite sets of variables; given
(L,K)\in D_{0}
, where
L=\llbracket X\rrbracket
and
K=\llbracket Y\rrbracket
,
L\otimes_{0}K=\llbracket X\cup Y\rrbracket
;
\mathsf{E}_{0}=[~]
.

For morphisms, its partial monoid structure
\langle D_{1},\otimes_{1},\mathsf{E}_{1}\rangle
is:
D_{1}=\{(f,g)\in\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]))\times\mathbf{ob}(\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta]))\mid f\oplus g\text{ is defined}\}
; given
(f,g)\in D_{1}
,
f\otimes_{1}g=f\oplus g
;
\mathsf{E}_{2}=\mathit{id}_{[~]}
.

With a bit abuse of notation, we shall simply denote both
\otimes_{0}
and
\otimes_{1}
simply by their corresponding operation
\oplus
.

Next, that
\langle D_{0},D_{1}\rangle
forms a subcategory
\mathbb{D}
of
\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta])\times\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta])
and
\oplus\colon\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{Ker}(\mathbb{C}[\theta])
is a functor follows from the frame conditions – in particular (
RevExchange
).

\square

Lemma 3

In a Markov category
\mathbb{X}
, superset CI implies Markov CI.

Proof

Given an
\mathbb{X}
-morphism
s\colon\mathsf{I}\to\mathsf{W}\otimes\mathsf{X}\otimes\mathsf{Y}\otimes\mathsf{U}
satisfying
\mathsf{X}\!\perp_{\!\mathrm{S}}\!\mathsf{Y}\!\mid\!\mathsf{W}
– i.e., it can be decomposed as in
Figure

4(b)
, we show that is also satisfies
\mathsf{X}\!\perp_{\!\mathrm{M}}\!\mathsf{Y}\!\mid\!\mathsf{W}
– i.e., it can be expressed as in
Figure

4(a)
.

See

Proof

Note that when
U=\varnothing
, both the superset CI statement
X\!\perp_{\!\mathrm{S}}\!Y\!\mid\!W
and the Markov CI statement
X\!\perp_{\!\mathrm{M}}\!Y\!\mid\!W
reduce to the plain CI statement
X\!\perp\!Y\!\mid\!W
. So the statement follows immediately from
Theorem

6.1
and
Lemma

3
.

\square

This precisely says that
s
satisfies Markov CI
\mathsf{X}\!\perp_{\!\mathrm{M}}\!\mathsf{Y}\!\mid\!\mathsf{W}
.

For the second part of the statement, note that
\mathbb{C}
has conditionals implies that
\mathbb{C}[\theta]
also has conditionals (
Proposition

10
). Then it follows immediately from the first half of the current statement together with
Theorem

6.1
.
